newsitem.title: USA: Management shakeup at Maine Yankee - source.
newsitem.headline: Management shakeup at Maine Yankee - source.

text.p: Management changes are planned for the Maine Yankee nuclear power plant which has been the focus of safety concerns and equipment problems, a state official said Friday.

The president of Maine Yankee's board of directors David Flanagan has scheduled a news conference for 1400 EST/1900 GMT today, but officials have declined to comment on the subject of his announcement.
The official, who asked to remain unnamed, told Reuters that Flannigan would announce a "management shakeup" but declined to provide additional details.

The 910-megawatt plant has been taken off-line repeatedly for the past two years as engineers correct problem ranging from cracked steam tube pipes to safety systems that had key electrical wires accidentally removed.

The plant has been off-line since Dec. 6 while engineers correct routing problems with control room electical cables. Maine Yankee officials have said they hopes to return the facility to operation in early January.

The Nuclear Regulatory Commission, whose concerns over improperly laid cabling led to the current outage, said in its daily report Friday that the plant's operators "will decide today if cooldown is necessary."

A cooldown would involve fully shutting the plant's reactor. A similar move was made at the Connecticut Yankee power station ahead of its owners' decision last month to permanently shut the unit for economic reasons.
Plant officials said this month that they would spend an additional $27 million on safety related concerns in 1997 after a special NRC inspection criticized Maine Yankee management.

The facility was shut down for nearly all of 1995 while engineers fixed cracks in the 24-year-old plant's steam generator. The $30 million repair project was the most extensive tube "resleaving" by a U.S. nuclear facility.

The inspection was requested by Gov. Angus King after an NRC investigation raised questions about whether Maine Yankee's emergency core cooling system was properly licensed during a power upgrade in the late 1980s.

The licensing issue is also being investigated by the Justice Department. An anonymous whistle-blower alleged in December 1995 that Maine Yankee's engineer's mislead the NRC about the adequacy of a computer code used to test the system. The plant has denied wrongdoing.

The plant has been restricted to 90 percent capacity while a new computer test is eing reveiwed. Gov. King has said he thinks it is unlikely the plant will be allowed to return to 100 percent capacity.

Maine Yankee is 38 percent owned by Central Maine Power Co, 20 percent each by New England Electric System and Northeast Utilities, seven percent by Bangor Hydro, five percent by Maine Public Service Co. and 10 percent by other New England utilities.
